slides.title: Curvature and Space Forms
slides.notes: Open by announcing the chapter's shift in scale. Previous chapters built connections, geodesics, and Riemannian metrics; this lecture asks what curvature data those structures carry and how much of that data is visible from two-dimensional planes. Keep the three model geometries on screen as the destination.

slides.title: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: Use this route to prevent the chapter from feeling like a list of propositions. The source span has four sections, but the instructional arc is one continuous compression story: curvature tensors are constrained objects, sectional curvature samples them, constant curvature collapses the tensor to one number, and flatness collapses it to holonomy.

slides.title: Algebraic Curvature Starts Before Manifolds
slides.notes: Stress that the chapter begins in a vector space because the curvature tensor at a point has algebraic life of its own. The skew rules and Bianchi identity are not decorative signs; they are filters that remove impossible components before geometry enters, making later sectional reconstruction believable.

slides.title: Planes Determine The Tensor
slides.notes: Present this as the chapter's first surprise. A single plane gives only one number, but the family of all planes is rich enough to reconstruct the algebraic tensor. This explains why the later definition of sectional curvature is not a weak substitute for R; it is a carefully chosen sampling device.

slides.title: Sectional Curvature On A Riemannian Manifold
slides.notes: Connect the abstract section to the manifold by freezing the geometry at one point. The Riemannian metric lets us choose orthonormal vectors and turn R into a scalar. Students should leave with the habit that sectional curvature is not attached to a direction alone, but to a two-dimensional tangent plane.

slides.title: Ricci Curvature Is A Sum Of Sectional Views
slides.notes: Use Ricci curvature as a bridge rather than a detour. The chapter introduces the symmetric bilinear form obtained by tracing the curvature tensor, and the proposition says exactly what that trace means for a unit vector: add the sectional curvatures of all planes that contain it.

slides.title: Constant Curvature Collapses R To One Function
slides.notes: Pause here because this formula is the hinge of the chapter. Algebraic Proposition 1.4 is being globalized: if the sectional curvature is independent of the plane at a point, then the tensor cannot hide any additional information. All remaining variation is the scalar function k on the manifold.

slides.title: Schur's Theorem Turns Pointwise Isotropy Into Constancy
slides.notes: State the theorem carefully, including connectedness and the dimension restriction. The proof is a good example of differential geometry using room: in dimension at least three, one can choose enough orthogonal vectors for the Bianchi identity to isolate directional derivatives of k. That is why the local scalar becomes global.

slides.title: Curvature Forms Record Constant Curvature Compactly
slides.notes: This slide ties the chapter back to the principal bundle language of earlier sections. In a space of constant curvature, the curvature form is not an arbitrary matrix of two-forms. Each entry is the wedge of canonical coframe components, multiplied by the same scalar k.

slides.title: Constructing The Simply Connected Models
slides.notes: Frame Theorem 3.1 as a construction theorem, not merely a catalog. For every constant curvature sign, the chapter builds a simply connected complete model. The proof uses quadrics, invariant quadratic forms, and the orthonormal frame bundle to compute the curvature form.

slides.title: The Quadric Formula Unifies Sphere And Hyperbolic Space
slides.notes: The quadric equation is the chapter's efficient model builder. Rather than memorize separate constructions, students can track the sign of r. Positive r produces the round sphere after a coordinate rescaling, while negative r produces hyperbolic components with a metric inherited from the indefinite ambient form.

slides.title: Homogeneity Comes From Preserving A Quadratic Form
slides.notes: Explain that homogeneity is not assumed after the models are written down; it follows from the group that preserves the quadratic form. The proof identifies this group with the orthonormal frame bundle in the model case, so the constant curvature calculation becomes a Maurer-Cartan computation.

slides.title: Space Forms Are Sorted By The Sign Of K
slides.notes: This is the classification language students should remember from the chapter's model section. Elliptic, hyperbolic, and flat are not just names for familiar pictures; they are sign classes for constant sectional curvature. Emphasize that the simply connected complete representatives are the local models for later space-form discussions.

slides.title: Flat Affine Connections Have Three Equivalent Faces
slides.notes: Make clear that flat affine does not initially mean Riemannian. The theorem gives three equivalent tests: a local model connection, vanishing torsion and curvature, and discrete affine holonomy. This is a good place to recall that the affine frame bundle contains translational information beyond the linear frame bundle.

slides.title: Flat Riemannian Examples Can Still Have Topology
slides.notes: Use the examples to separate local curvature from global topology. Euclidean cylinders and tori inherit flat metrics from Euclidean space, but the chapter also includes a flat affine torus that is not Riemannian. This distinction prepares students for the covering-space theorem that follows.

slides.title: Complete Flat Affine Manifolds Lift To Ordinary Affine Space
slides.notes: The theorem is easiest to teach as a covering ladder. Completeness lets the universal flat affine model be ordinary affine space. Factoring by the translation kernel produces a Euclidean cylinder, while the remaining linear holonomy accounts for the passage down to the original manifold.

slides.title: Compact Flat Riemannian Manifolds Have Torus Covers
slides.notes: Keep the proof details at the level of architecture unless the course wants a group-theory digression. The compactness assumption forces enough translations to create a torus cover, and the remaining linear holonomy is finite. This is the chapter's compact flat Riemannian classification theme.

slides.title: Two-Dimensional Flat Manifolds: Four Quotient Patterns
slides.notes: Use the surface list as an accessible finish to a highly abstract chapter. The universal cover is the Euclidean plane, but the allowed deck transformations determine the surface type. Orientation-preserving translations produce cylinders and tori, while adding a flip produces the twisted cylinder and Klein bottle.
